newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: West losing textile jobs, output shift to Asia - ILO.
newsitem.headline: West losing textile jobs, output shift to Asia - ILO.

text.p: Employment in textiles, clothing and footwear industries has slumped by more than 40 percent in the past two decades in the West as output shifts to developing countries, the International Labour Organisation said on Monday.
"Much of production capacity and jobs have shifted to the developing world," the Geneva-based U.N. agency said in a new report on trends in the three industries.
The ILO said Asia led the surge in jobs with a growth rate of 597 percent in Malaysia, 416 percent in Bangladesh, 385 percent in Sri Lanka and 334 percent in Indonesia in 1970-1990.

In sharp contrast, the number of workers in textiles, clothing and footwear industries slumped in the developed world in the same period -- down 58 percent in Germany, 55 percent in Britain, 49 percent in France and 31 percent in the U.S.
Between 1980 and 1993, the ILO said Finland suffered the highest fall in employment with 72 percent, followed by Sweden and Norway with 65 percent each and Austria with 52 percent.

In the same period, Mauritius led the growth in employment with a whopping 345 percent, followed by Indonesia with 177 percent, Morocco with 167 percent, Jordan with 161 percent and Jamaica and Malaysia with 101 percent each, the agency said.
The United States employs 1.6 million workers in the three sectors, down from 2.5 million in 1980, compared to 5.3 million in China, up two million over the figure for 1980, the ILO said.
The agency said more than 60 percent of world clothing exports came from developing countries. Asia had the biggest share with 32 percent. China led world exports with a 13-percent share.

In textiles, although industrialised countries still lead the global output, the countries were able to achieve an average annual production growth rate of only 0.2 percent in the past two decades against 3.6 percent in Asia, the ILO said.
A production shift to informal sectors also helped create more jobs in developing countries, the agency said.
The ILO also noted a gradual shift to part-time and temporary jobs in the industry from full-time in-plant jobs.
The report estimated the total number of jobs in the formal sector at 23.6 million but noted that jobs in the informal sector could be ten times as high.
"No one knows just how many work in the informal sector but the figure may be five to ten times as high," Kari Tapiola, deputy director-general of the ILO, said in the report.
